paragraphs: Joint image alignment tries to undo unwanted deformations across a collection so that shared patterns line up. Image Congealing approaches this by making the aligned collection simpler, for example by reducing the variability at each pixel. Its attraction is that it does not require an explicit model describing what the aligned images should look like.

Simplicity alone, however, can reward an unhelpful result: transformations may collapse the images into something constant. Conventional Image Congealing must explicitly constrain transformations to exclude such solutions. This paper instead balances the complexity of the aligned collection against fidelity to the information in the original data. Alignment should remove unwanted variation while retaining useful content.

The resulting formulation addresses the collapse problem through the objective itself, eliminating the need for explicit transformation regularization. The authors also identify noise suppression as a useful property and demonstrate modeling and computational benefits on some problems previously addressed with Image Congealing. The contribution is a more principled criterion for deciding which simplifications count as successful alignment.
neurips-2006-a-complexity-distortion-app.tldr: Balancing information preservation against simplicity makes joint image alignment less vulnerable to collapsed solutions.

paragraphs: Switching linear dynamical systems describe sequences that move between different patterns of linear evolution. A hidden switch selects the active dynamics, while a continuous hidden state generates observations. Smoothing estimates those hidden quantities using the entire observed sequence, including later observations. Exact inference becomes intractable because the possibilities grow exponentially with sequence length.

The paper introduces an approximate Gaussian Sum smoother that also handles switches whose transitions depend on the continuous hidden state. It removes a key approximation used by the standard Kim smoother, allowing future observations to contribute more fully. Its central approximation is to represent the relevant distributions through mixtures of Gaussians. Adding a conditional independence assumption yields a simpler alternative reported to remain stable and accurate.

The procedure requires one forward pass and one backward pass, resembling smoothing corrections in ordinary linear dynamical systems. The authors report good performance on toy experiments and a large speech recognition application involving noise. The contribution combines richer use of future evidence with a direct computation that avoids the unstable Expectation Propagation alternative discussed in the abstract.
neurips-2006-a-novel-gaussian-sum-smooth.tldr: A Gaussian mixture smoother uses future observations more fully for approximate inference in switching dynamical systems.

paragraphs: Efficient coding theories can produce receptive fields resembling those in primary visual cortex, yet fail to explain retinal responses. This paper asks whether the retina is optimizing a different combination of objectives. The signal reaching it has already been blurred by the eye's optics and corrupted by photoreceptor noise, so preserving information alone does not capture every relevant demand.

The authors develop a theoretical framework that combines removal of blur and noise with robustness to neural noise and effective use of the available neurons. These requirements concern the population as a whole: the code must distribute useful visual information across a limited collection of noisy units while accounting for degradation at the input.

When optimized for natural images, the model produces filters strongly resembling retinal ganglion cell receptive fields. Their characteristics also vary with retinal eccentricity, where optical blur and ganglion cell numbers differ. The model therefore offers a unified account connecting retinal coding to these conditions. More generally, the authors interpret it as extending Wiener filtering to an arbitrary number of noisy units.
neurips-2006-a-theory-of-retinal-populat.tldr: A theory balancing image restoration, neural noise, and neuron availability produces filters resembling retinal receptive fields.

paragraphs: This paper studies the probability that an AdaBoost classifier makes an error, focusing on how training should stop as the sample size increases. The central question is consistency: whether classifiers trained on increasingly large samples can approach the lowest error achievable for the underlying prediction problem. That benchmark is called the Bayes risk.

The stated result connects consistency to a stopping strategy whose iteration count depends on the training sample size. Under that strategy, the sequence of classifier risks approaches the Bayes risk when the Bayes risk is strictly positive. The supplied abstract has an incomplete rendering of the stopping formula, so its exact schedule cannot be reliably reconstructed from this evidence.

The significance is that stopping is part of the theoretical guarantee, rather than merely a choice about training time. The result concerns convergence of prediction error as more data become available. It does not promise zero error: with positive Bayes risk, even the best possible classifier has unavoidable error. AdaBoost's stated achievement is approaching that benchmark under the specified stopping condition.
neurips-2006-adaboost-is-consistent-a45a.tldr: AdaBoost's error approaches positive Bayes risk under a sample-size-dependent stopping strategy.

paragraphs: An agent facing a complex environment cannot perform unlimited computation before choosing how to act. This paper studies that constraint through games in which each strategy carries an additional cost. The cost may represent computation or another expense associated with the strategy. This makes the burden of choosing and using a strategy part of the strategic problem itself.

The authors first investigate games that are zero-sum before these strategy costs are added. They prove a generalization of the classical min-max theorem for this setting, describing the result as counterintuitive. They also examine potential games and establish that adding strategy costs preserves their status as potential games.

A shared consequence is that simple learning dynamics converge to equilibrium in both of the studied settings with strategy costs. This matters because bounded rationality raises questions about both desirable decisions and how agents can reach stable behavior. The model provides a way to incorporate resource costs while retaining convergence properties for these particular game families.
neurips-2006-an-approach-to-bounded-rati.tldr: Adding strategy costs models bounded rationality while preserving equilibrium convergence in the studied game families.

paragraphs: A classifier trained on one distribution may need to operate on another. Domain adaptation studies this situation: labeled examples come from a source domain, while useful predictions are needed in a different target domain. The paper asks what makes such transfer possible and focuses on the representation used to describe the data.

The authors formalize the importance of representation through a generalization bound for domain adaptation. The theory exposes tradeoffs in choosing features for transfer, giving a mathematical basis for evaluating a representation beyond its usefulness on source examples alone. It also supplies a new justification for a previously proposed adaptation model.

The analysis points toward another model that simultaneously reduces the difference between source and target domains and increases the training margin. In plain terms, it seeks a representation in which the domains become more alike while the labeled training classes remain well separated. The abstract presents this as a promising direction motivated by the theory, rather than as a reported empirical victory for the proposed model.
neurips-2006-analysis-of-representations.tldr: A generalization bound explains representation tradeoffs in transferring classifiers between different data distributions.

paragraphs: Clustering often benefits from prior knowledge about which observations should belong together. This paper develops a probabilistic formulation that incorporates such grouping information. It has two interpretations: a finite mixture model with a grouping prior, or penalized logistic regression in which labels are observed only indirectly through the probability distributions associated with the classes.

The authors derive a generalized expectation-maximization algorithm for estimating the model parameters. Its expectation step has a closed-form solution. This is a practical distinction from the recent probabilistic clustering approaches discussed in the abstract, which rely on Gibbs sampling or shortcuts described as suboptimal to carry out their inference.

Image segmentation is a central application because spatial relationships can guide the grouping of image regions. The formulation avoids the combinatorial character of Markov random field priors and permits more sophisticated spatial priors, including wavelet-based ones, in a computationally efficient way. The authors also extend the framework to unsupervised, semi-supervised, and discriminative modes, allowing related modeling machinery to serve different levels of label availability.
neurips-2006-clustering-under-prior-know.tldr: A probabilistic clustering framework incorporates grouping knowledge with efficient inference and flexible spatial priors.

paragraphs: Large datasets often contain mostly zero entries, making sparsity an important property for approximation methods to exploit. This paper introduces Conditional Random Sampling, or CRS, which combines sketching with sampling. A sketch serves as a compact representation of the data, and CRS turns that representation into conditional random samples during estimation.

A distinguishing feature is that the sample size is determined retrospectively. Sampling is therefore tied to the estimation stage rather than being described solely as a fixed preprocessing choice. The paper focuses on using this mechanism to approximate pairwise l1 and l2 distances, two ways of measuring how far apart data vectors are.

The authors compare CRS with random projections. For Boolean data, whose entries are zero or one, they establish a theoretical advantage over random projections. On real-world data, they report that CRS often performs better, a qualified empirical finding rather than a claim about every dataset. The method is positioned for applications where approximate comparisons support learning, data mining, information retrieval, or database query optimization.
neurips-2006-conditional-random-sampling.tldr: Conditional Random Sampling converts sketches into samples for distance estimation, with a proven advantage over random projections on Boolean data.

paragraphs: Classification becomes demanding when a model must distinguish among a large collection of related categories. This paper proposes an efficient framework for kernel multiclass models designed for that setting. Its target is a structured set of classes, with hierarchical text classification providing the demonstrated application.

The framework learns kernel parameters automatically by maximizing cross-validation log likelihood. This makes performance on held-out portions of the training data part of the parameter-selection objective. Because the criterion concerns likelihood, it evaluates the probabilities assigned to outcomes rather than only whether the selected class is correct. The framework also estimates predictive probabilities for its classifications.

On large text classification tasks with hierarchical classes, the authors report state-of-the-art results in roughly one tenth of the time taken by previous work. The stated contribution thus combines predictive performance with reduced computation in the evaluated setting. It also brings automatic kernel tuning and probability estimation into one framework, making model selection a central part of the proposed approach to large structured classification problems.
neurips-2006-cross-validation-optimizati.tldr: Automatic cross-validation tuning enables efficient kernel classification across large hierarchies, with strong reported text-classification results.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning models contain settings that govern how quickly learning occurs, how future rewards are valued, and how behavior balances exploration with exploitation. This paper investigates whether changes in these meta-parameters can describe differences in animal learning associated with stress and genetic background. Their relationship to brain neuromodulators is presented as a hypothesis.

The authors studied C57BL/6 and DBA/2 mice in light conditioning using a five-hole box and in the Morris water maze. Different stress conditions allowed them to examine immediate performance and long-term memory. They then simulated behavior with reinforcement learning models, fitting a set of meta-parameters separately for each experimental session.

Several fitted meta-parameters showed qualitatively similar dynamics across the two simulated experiments, alongside statistically significant differences between strains and stress conditions. These findings support the use of dynamically controlled reinforcement learning settings to describe many aspects of the observed behavior. The fitted values provide a computational account of behavioral differences; the abstract does not establish them as direct measurements of neuromodulator levels.
neurips-2006-effects-of-stress-and-genot.tldr: Changing reinforcement learning meta-parameters describes behavioral differences associated with mouse genotype and stress conditions.

paragraphs: Kernel principal component analysis can be computed iteratively using the Kernel Hebbian Algorithm, or KHA. The paper identifies its gain parameter, which controls update sizes, as a source of slow convergence. Conventional KHA uses a single gain that either remains constant or decreases according to a fixed schedule.

The first proposed improvement, KHA/et, replaces that scalar with a gain vector based on reciprocals of the currently estimated eigenvalues. This makes update scaling depend on the components being learned. The second improvement derives and applies Stochastic MetaDescent to KHA/et, adapting gains in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space in which the kernel method operates.

Experiments cover kernel PCA and spectral clustering of USPS digits, along with motion capture and image denoising problems. The authors report substantially faster convergence than conventional KHA, with the additional adaptation further accelerating the first improvement. The contribution concerns how efficiently the iterative procedure approaches its solution: adaptive update sizes make better use of the evolving estimates than the conventional scalar gain choices.
neurips-2006-fast-iterative-kernel-pca-1.tldr: Eigenvalue-based gains and further gain adaptation substantially accelerate iterative kernel PCA in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering often builds a graph from local similarities and uses a few global eigenvectors to divide the data into groups. This paper examines limitations of that progression from local relationships to a global partition. It shows that local information alone does not make the normalized cut objective a suitable measure of clustering quality.

A separate problem persists even with a suitable similarity measure: the first few eigenvectors can fail to recover groups that differ in size and density. The issue is therefore not solely how similarities are chosen. It also concerns which structures the limited spectral representation can capture when several scales coexist.

The authors propose a diffusion-based measure of the coherence of individual clusters. It is scale-free and can be paired with any bottom-up graph-based clustering method to identify coherent groups across scales. Synthetic examples and image segmentation problems illustrate failures of several spectral methods, while the proposed coherence measure finds the expected groups at all scales in those examples. The contribution combines a diagnosis of spectral limitations with a different criterion for evaluating clusters.
neurips-2006-fundamental-limitations-of-.tldr: The paper identifies multiscale failures of spectral clustering and proposes a diffusion-based measure of cluster coherence.

paragraphs: Kernel learning makes the choice of kernel part of the learning problem. This paper contributes a new method for constructing hyperkernels, which provide machinery for learning kernels themselves. The focus is on how that machinery can be specified in a usable form and how it can support several kinds of learning tasks.

The authors define two special cases, called Gaussian and Wishart hyperkernels, that can be computed in closed form. This gives explicit constructions for these cases. They single out the Gaussian hyperkernel because its regularization scheme has an interpretable character reminiscent of the familiar Gaussian radial basis function kernel.

The paper also broadens the role assigned to kernel learning. Beyond improving classification and regression methods, it discusses using kernel learning as a standalone approach to dimensionality reduction and relational or metric learning. In these uses, learning the representation of relationships is itself a goal. The stated contribution is the construction and interpretation of these hyperkernels, together with an account of their potential roles across these tasks.
neurips-2006-gaussian-and-wishart-hyperk.tldr: Gaussian and Wishart hyperkernels provide closed-form constructions for kernel learning and its broader representation-learning uses.

paragraphs: Maximum margin clustering adapts the separation principle of support vector machines to data without labels. The paper identifies three obstacles in the existing approach: a parameter count that grows quadratically with the number of examples, a restriction forcing clustering boundaries through the origin, and sensitivity to kernel choices that require external parameter selection.

The proposed generalized framework addresses these issues together. It permits boundaries that do not pass through the origin, removing the restriction associated with difficulties on unbalanced datasets. It reduces the number of parameters to improve computational efficiency and can determine an appropriate kernel matrix automatically without labeled examples.

The authors also establish a formal connection between maximum margin clustering and spectral clustering, relating two approaches to discovering groups. Experiments on synthetic data and real datasets from the UCI repository demonstrate the efficiency of the generalized algorithm. Its practical significance lies in combining more flexible boundaries, reduced optimization burden, and unsupervised kernel selection within one framework, rather than treating those concerns as separate preprocessing and tuning tasks.
neurips-2006-generalized-maximum-margin-.tldr: Generalized maximum margin clustering adds flexible boundaries, fewer parameters, and automatic kernel learning without labels.

paragraphs: Some network observations reveal which nodes participated in a pathway without recording their order. This occurs in biological and communication systems where precise timing can be difficult to obtain. Recovering connections from such observations is challenging because every ordering of the observed nodes gives another feasible explanation, creating a combinatorially large set of possibilities.

The paper introduces a probabilistic model that treats each observed co-occurrence as a randomly shuffled sample from a random walk on the network. It builds on the intuition that nodes appearing together more often are likely to be more closely connected. This model assigns structure to the missing-order problem instead of treating all feasible pathways as equally likely.

The authors derive an efficient network inference algorithm and analyze a Monte Carlo version using new concentration inequalities for importance sampling estimates. They prove high-probability convergence for a version with polynomial complexity. The result supports computationally manageable inference under the proposed model; convergence of the algorithm is the stated guarantee, rather than unconditional recovery of every network from unordered observations.
neurips-2006-inferring-network-structure.tldr: Modeling unordered node co-occurrences as shuffled random walks enables efficient network inference with a high-probability convergence guarantee.

paragraphs: Sensory processing may benefit from separating mixed input into statistically independent components, producing a less redundant description of the world. Another useful goal is to preferentially preserve components related to a second information source, such as an internal prediction or feedback about body position. The paper connects this second goal to information bottleneck optimization.

These are abstract objectives for unsupervised learning, but implementing them with neurons that communicate through spikes requires concrete learning rules. The authors derive a new rule from information optimization principles and show how it can support both independent component extraction and information bottleneck optimization in stochastically spiking neurons with refractoriness.

The result bridges a description of what information a representation should retain with a model of how spiking neurons could learn it. Refractoriness is part of the neuronal setting in which the construction is presented. The claim is explicitly one of possibility: these computations can in principle be implemented in the proposed kind of neuron. It does not establish that biological sensory systems necessarily use the derived rule.
neurips-2006-information-bottleneck-opti.tldr: A derived learning rule shows how stochastic spiking neurons could implement information bottleneck optimization and independent component extraction.

paragraphs: Structural equation models extend Gaussian belief networks to graphs that can contain cycles. The paper gives them a generative interpretation: they can describe the joint distribution of long-term average equilibrium activity in Gaussian dynamic belief networks. This links a model of averaged activity to an underlying process that evolves over time.

In fMRI analysis, researchers often specify a network structure first and compare its fitted parameters across groups. The authors argue that learning structure can also be worthwhile when prior structural knowledge is incomplete or uncertain and sufficient data are available. They demonstrate structure learning on a toy problem and find that commonly assumed simple models are unsupported for the particular fMRI data examined.

The paper reports that learned structural equation models can be sensible and offer modeling benefits, while emphasizing that they need not match the true causal network. This distinction matters for interpreting connectivity. The authors suggest that combining prior models with learning, or incorporating temporal information through dynamic models, may offer greater benefits than learning structural equations alone.
neurips-2006-learning-structural-equatio.tldr: Learning fMRI network structure can improve modeling, but the resulting structural equations need not reveal the true causal network.

paragraphs: Search ranking measures often depend on document order rather than the numerical scores that produced it. Small score changes may leave the order unchanged, while an order change can produce a discontinuity. Consequently, derivatives of the ranking cost with respect to model parameters can be zero or undefined, obstructing direct optimization.

The paper introduces LambdaRank, a family of algorithms that works with implicit cost functions to avoid these difficulties. It describes the approach using neural networks, while stating that it applies to any differentiable function class. The authors provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the implicit cost to be convex and give the method a mechanical interpretation.

Across several datasets, the authors report significantly improved accuracy over a state-of-the-art ranking algorithm. They also show that LambdaRank can significantly accelerate that algorithm's training. These results make the approach relevant to both ranking quality and computational effort. Although ranking motivates the paper, the proposed method is described as extendable to other nonsmooth, multivariate costs, broadening the potential use of its implicit-objective approach.
neurips-2006-learning-to-rank-with-nonsm.tldr: LambdaRank uses implicit costs to train ranking models despite nondifferentiable ranking measures, improving reported accuracy and training speed.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning algorithm must choose actions while it is still learning which choices are valuable. This paper evaluates that ongoing behavior in an undiscounted setting, where future rewards are not progressively reduced by a discount factor. Its focus is performance after a finite number of interactions, rather than only the quality of an eventual learned policy.

The proposed algorithm, UCRL, uses upper confidence bounds to manage the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. The approach draws on methods used successfully for multi-armed bandit problems. Confidence bounds provide a way to make decisions that account for uncertainty, connecting the need to gather information with the goal of obtaining rewards during learning.

The authors establish logarithmic online regret in the number of steps relative to an optimal policy. Regret measures the accumulated performance shortfall against that reference. A logarithmic bound means this shortfall grows slowly as interaction continues, giving a quantitative account of the cost of learning while acting. The contribution is a finite-step performance guarantee for the presented undiscounted reinforcement learning algorithm.
neurips-2006-logarithmic-online-regret-b.tldr: UCRL uses upper confidence bounds to achieve logarithmic online regret in the studied undiscounted reinforcement learning setting.

paragraphs: Robots planning together may have goals that partly overlap without being identical. Cooperation can benefit all participants, but they still need to select a mutually acceptable plan and have reasons to follow it. The paper addresses this combination of planning, negotiation, and incentives in general-sum stochastic games.

The authors identify a gap between two research traditions. Multi-agent planning often leaves aside whether every participant has an incentive to carry out a proposed agreement. Game-theoretic algorithms address incentives but can struggle with large planning problems. The paper proposes an efficient approximate game-theoretic planning algorithm to help connect these concerns.

A negotiation protocol accompanies the algorithm and encourages agents to compute and agree on joint plans that are fair and optimal according to the paper's definitions. The method concerns approximating subgame-perfect equilibria, bringing continued incentives into the planning problem. Demonstrations use two simple robotic planning tasks. These illustrate the combined algorithm and protocol; the abstract's efficiency claim and demonstrations should not be read as evidence of deployment across arbitrary large robotic systems.
neurips-2006-multi-robot-negotiation-app.tldr: An approximate game-theoretic planner and negotiation protocol help robots agree on cooperative plans with incentives to follow them.

paragraphs: Seeing depth from two eyes requires resolving ambiguous matches between their images. Computational models suggest that local competition rejects poor matches while cooperation over longer distances helps refine a consistent interpretation. This paper tests predictions about these interactions by recording several neurons simultaneously in primary visual cortex, or V1, of awake, behaving macaques.

The animals viewed surfaces at different depths represented by dynamic random dot stereograms. Interactions between pairs of neurons depended on both similarities in their receptive fields and the presented stimulus. Neurons coding the same depth shared early inhibition when the stimulus had a disparity they did not prefer. Later, they showed mutual facilitation when the stimulus matched their preferred disparity.

This timing is consistent with a process in which competition first removes gross mismatches and cooperation subsequently sharpens depth estimates. The findings connect patterns of neuronal interaction to proposed computational roles, going beyond the responses of isolated neurons. They support the cooperative account, while the abstract carefully describes them as consistent with that mechanism rather than as uniquely proving it.
neurips-2006-neurophysiological-evidence.tldr: Early inhibition and later facilitation among V1 neurons support competitive and cooperative mechanisms for estimating depth.

paragraphs: Single-class classification asks how to recognize a target class when the learning problem centers on that class. This paper studies an idealized version as a game between a learner and an adversary. The learner is assumed to know the complete target distribution, giving the analysis a stronger starting point than ordinary learning from a finite sample.

The objective is to guarantee a specified tolerance for false-positive errors while making false-negative errors as small as possible. For different versions of the game, the authors identify optimal hard and soft classification strategies. They show that soft classification can offer a significant advantage, so the form of the classifier can matter even when the target distribution is already known.

The resulting strategies and bounds also inform more conventional single-class learning. In particular, they provide worst-case lower bounds for finite-sample problems, establishing benchmarks for what those problems can achieve. The analysis additionally motivates new approaches to classification. Its value lies in separating the strategic difficulty of the decision problem from the extra uncertainty introduced by having only sampled data.
neurips-2006-optimal-single-class-classi.tldr: A game-theoretic analysis derives optimal single-class classifiers and shows that soft strategies can have a significant advantage.

paragraphs: Multinomial logistic regression predicts membership across several classes. Sparse versions are useful when identifying informative features matters alongside prediction, as in text processing and microarray classification. This paper proposes a Bayesian approach that encourages sparsity while changing how the strength of that encouragement is handled.

The model uses a Laplace prior to produce sparse coefficients. A usual regularization parameter controls the amount of regularization, but here the authors integrate that parameter out analytically. This incorporates it into the mathematical treatment instead of selecting its value through the cross-validation procedure used for comparison. The method thus targets a computational burden associated with fitting a sparse multiclass model.

Across benchmark datasets, the authors report generalization performance similar to that obtained using cross-validation, at greatly reduced computational expense. The finding concerns maintaining comparable prediction on unseen data while making model fitting less costly. It supports analytical treatment of the regularization parameter as a practical alternative in the evaluated problems, while retaining the sparse formulation that makes informative features explicit.
neurips-2006-sparse-multinomial-logistic.tldr: Analytically integrating out regularization strength yields sparse multiclass logistic regression with comparable generalization at lower reported computational cost.

paragraphs: Speakers sometimes have a choice between marking a phrase with an extra word and leaving that marker out. This paper uses such syntactic reduction to investigate whether language production tends to spread information more evenly across an utterance. The motivating hypothesis is that speakers may structure language to improve its communicative properties.

The authors find that less information-dense phrases are more likely to be reduced. This pattern fits the idea that optional wording is less useful where the upcoming content is already predictable. They then combine a stochastic model of structured utterance production with logistic regression to examine what information speakers use when judging that predictability.

The tendency toward predictability-sensitive reduction remains robust across a wide variety of control variables. The analysis also provides evidence that speakers use both surface cues and structural cues when estimating what comes next. Together, the findings connect optional grammatical choices to information distribution. They support a tendency compatible with more uniform information density, rather than establishing that every utterance is globally optimized.
neurips-2006-speakers-optimize-informati.tldr: Speakers reduce less information-dense phrases more often, using both surface and structural cues to estimate predictability.

paragraphs: Coordinated neural oscillations provide a timing reference against which a neuron's firing phase can represent an analog quantity. This paper asks how such a representation could also express uncertainty. A remembered value is more useful when a system can distinguish a precise estimate from one supported only weakly.

The proposed idea uses the fact that a neuron need not fire exactly once during each oscillation cycle: it can fire several times or remain silent. The degree to which its spikes concentrate around a phase could report uncertainty about the represented quantity. This links information in spike timing to a possible representation of confidence within the same oscillatory system.

The authors apply the theory to a model of oscillatory associative memory recall in hippocampal area CA3. Within that model, the theory supports viewing retrieval as a process that represents and manipulates uncertainty as well as recalling content. The contribution is a proposed coding account and its application to a memory model; the abstract presents phase concentration as a possible mechanism rather than an established biological measurement rule.
neurips-2006-uncertainty-phase-and-oscil.tldr: A theory proposes that spike-phase concentration could encode uncertainty during oscillatory hippocampal memory recall.
